article.plain_text:
I have been thinking deeply about what attitude I ought to take toward substance misuse.Increasingly, I have come to realize that what I am confronting is not a simple question of right and wrong, or good and bad, but a profound moral dilemma.
 Because one fact is difficult to deny: for some people who have been pushed into extreme isolation, deprived of support, left with no viable alternatives, and driven by desperation, the experiences produced by harmful substances may at certain moments serve a distorted and dangerous, yet subjectively very real, psychological function. They may come to feel like the only thing keeping that person alive.
 That is where the contradiction lies.
 I know this from my own experience.
 It did, to some extent, comfort me.
 But later, it also harmed me deeply.
 And because I have experienced it myself, I understand all too well how severe the consequences of substance misuse can be.
 But suppose that, when confronted with substance misuse, there are only two options.
 Option A: STOP THEM.
 You keep the person away from substance misuse and its consequences, but leave them to continue enduring a reality they already find unbearable.
 Morally, this may seem like the unquestionably correct choice. Yet in practice, if no meaningful help is available, the only alternative that person feels they have left may be death.
 Option B: ALLOW IT.
 You respect the person's choice to use substances as a means of escaping unbearable pain, but in doing so you allow someone who is already in a severe crisis to face still greater risks, enormous financial costs, and potentially even more devastating consequences later on.
 This, too, is morally troubling.
 And yet, in that particular moment, it may appear to be the only lifeline they have left.
 Of course, what we really want is an Option C:
 That this person could live a healthy and safe life.
 That their simple—and perhaps not excessive at all—needs and wishes could actually be met: that they could live as the gender they know themselves to be; that they could be free from bullying at school and violence at home; that they could receive even a small amount of affirmation and find some reason to keep living; or that they could gain access to effective psychiatric and psychological care.
 Clearly, this would be the best answer.
 But perhaps the cruelest thing about reality is that sometimes the menu of available choices is so limited that there is simply no “Option C” on it.
 Perhaps, then, we should not blame people for failing to choose the “right” answer.
 Perhaps we should recognize instead that reality never gave them a menu containing Option C in the first place, and then forced them to choose between two desperate alternatives.
 And when detached spectators, standing somewhere safe, ask accusingly:
 “You should have chosen A.”
 or:
 “You should never have chosen B.”
 the person trapped inside that dilemma may be entirely justified in asking:
 “Why am I the one who has to bear responsibility for a moral dilemma created by society as a whole?”
 The risks of substance misuse do not disappear simply because a person's circumstances are tragic. But neither do that person's suffering and autonomy lose their ethical weight simply because substance misuse carries serious risks and costs.
 We should certainly do everything we can to reduce the former. But we should not invoke “protection” or “morality” as a justification for ignoring the latter.
 The deeper question—the one that deserves far more reflection—is not merely why a desperate person would choose a brief escape despite its enormous risks and costs.
 It is this:
 What drove that person into a position where desperation and harmful choices seemed to be the only choices left?
 In this sense, many people struggling with substance misuse remind me of The Little Match Girl.
 When the little girl struck her matches, she saw food, a warm stove, a Christmas tree, and her grandmother.
 Those visions, of course, were not physically real.
 But the reasons she saw them were not unreal at all.
 The vision was unreal; the deprivation was not.
 The stove was imaginary; the cold was not.
 Her grandmother was absent; her need for love was not.
 At the heart of substance misuse, there is often a person who has been driven to rely on something harmful and unreal—on an altered and distorted experience of reality—to temporarily satisfy a need that may itself be entirely real, understandable, and not excessive at all.
 Just as in the fairy tale, the matches really did give the Little Match Girl brief moments of warmth and beautiful visions.
 But the deeper cause of the tragedy—of her freezing to death in the street—was not simply that the matches eventually ran out.
 Nor can the tragedy be adequately explained merely by saying that winter was cold.
 The more fundamental question is:
 Why had she been left in a situation where matches were the only source of warmth available to her in the first place?
 And so a genuinely humane answer—one that actually addresses the heart of the problem—cannot consist only of saying:
 “Do not light matches to keep yourself warm.”
 It must go on to ask:
 “Why is she out there in the snow?”
 What a humane society—one that genuinely takes responsibility for the problem—should do is not merely “encourage” her to become more resilient so that she can endure the cold for a little longer.
 It should bring her in from the snow.
 It should give her the warm room she should have had all along.
 She does not need a box of matches that burns longer.
 She deserves a world in which she does not need matches to keep herself warm.
 Likewise,
 What people struggling with substance misuse ultimately deserve is not merely a safer match—not simply substances that are “less harmful” or “more effective”—but a world in which they no longer have to rely on substances to meet basic human needs in the first place.What they deserve is a world in which they do not have to misuse any substance in order to obtain the safety, dignity, love, relief, belonging, or happiness that should have been available to them without it.
 When people are given nothing but terrible options—when they are cornered until the only paths they can see are desperate and destructive ones—the responsibility for what follows cannot be placed entirely on the person who was forced to choose.
 Society, too, must bear responsibility for creating the conditions in which such choices came to seem like the only choices available.
 We need to confront and acknowledge the fact that their lives could have contained rescue, recovery, dignity, and countless other possibilities.
 Their fate was never destined to be an inevitable descent into an endless abyss of condemnation, incomprehension, and darkness.
